extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and general readers interested in poetic theory and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing lyric/narrative poetry that uses the real language of ordinary people, chooses humble subjects (especially rural life), and balances powerful feeling with thought and metrical restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthy purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Each poem should have a 'worthy purpose' rather than be merely trivial or ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth asserts that the Poems in the volumes are 'distinguished at least by one mark of difference, that each of them has a worthy purpose.' Avoid writing that lacks an aim; a good poem should illustrate something important about human feeling or nature rather than being mere verbal display. Anti-pattern: verses that are structurally competent but 'contemptible' because their matter lacks sense or capacity to excite thought (Dr. Johnson parody example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose incidents of common life (esp. low and rustic life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make incidents of common life interesting by tracing the primary laws of our nature; low and rustic life is especially suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rural and humble situations are recommended because 'the essential passions of the heart find a better soil' there: passions are less restrained, feelings more simple and durable, manners germinate from elementary feelings, and language is often nearer to original sources. Use such subjects to reveal elementary human passions and moral relations (e.g., maternal passion, fraternal attachment, death in childhood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the real language of men (avoid poetic diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use language near to the language of ordinary people; avoid conventional 'poetic diction' and artificial ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth recommends imitating and adopting 'the very language of men,' purified from true defects but stripped of conventional poetic phrases and fashions: 'little of what is usually called poetic diction.' Examples: avoid stock phrases that have been 'foolishly repeated by bad Poets.' Anti-patterns include indulging in arbitrary, capricious expressions intended to show off poetic learning rather than communicate feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personification of abstract ideas in these poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in rare instances, do not personify abstractions because such personifications are not part of real human language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth doesn't condemn all personification but says that in these poems he 'propose[s] to myself to imitate... the very language of men' and therefore largely abstains from personifications which don't naturally occur in ordinary speech. Use personification only when it arises naturally from feeling or when it serves the poem's purpose without falsifying the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and 'prosaisms' are acceptable when well-executed
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no essential difference between prose and metrical language except metre; lines that resemble good prose are not inherently defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics who denounce 'prosaisms' are mistaken: the language of much good poetry can be the language of well-written prose (illustrated by a Gray sonnet example). The test is whether the matter and feeling are interesting, not whether the diction sounds elevated. Anti-pattern: rejecting lines solely because they resemble prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings; 'emotion recollected in tranquillity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry originates from strong emotion that has been contemplated in tranquillity and then re-experienced in composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition generally begins in a mood where past emotion is recalled and transformed: 'The emotion is contemplated till... an emotion... is gradually produced.' Successful poems are produced in this state—writers should aim to write from 'emotion recollected in tranquillity' rather than raw, untempered outburst.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought must modulate feeling; poet needs meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although poetry springs from feeling, valuable poetry is produced by a mind that has 'thought long and deeply' about those feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feelings are 'modified and directed by our thoughts' which represent past feelings; deliberate contemplation allows the poet to discover what is important and to nourish feelings connected with important subjects. Anti-pattern: pure impulsive writing without intellectual shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce excitement tempered by an overbalance of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of poetry is to produce excitement, but this must coexist with an overbalance of pleasure—painful feeling should not overwhelm the reader's enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conveying powerful passions, ensure the reader's overall experience remains pleasurable. The 'music of harmonious metrical language' and associations with past pleasurable readings help temper painful descriptions. Evaluate passages for whether they raise excitement without tipping into distress that reduces pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metre and rhyme as structural aids that temper passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and rhyme are regular, reliable devices that can restrain or heighten passion and provide pleasurable impulses to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter supplies 'small, but continual and regular impulses of pleasurable surprise' which can keep pathos within pleasurable bounds; metre can also increase the power of otherwise modest subjects. Choose metrical patterns appropriate to the passion and movement of the poem; misuse (grossly injudicious metre) can fail to achieve the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The feeling should give importance to the action/situation, not the reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic feeling should illuminate and lend importance to actions and situations, rather than inventing significance for trivial events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth emphasizes that in his poems 'the feeling therein developed gives importance to the action and situation and not the action and situation to the feeling.' Avoid treating insignificant actions as grand merely to showcase emotion; instead, let authentic feeling reveal why an action or situation matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language must be fitted to the respective importance of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ideas in language appropriate to their weight; avoid falsehood of description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 'little falsehood of description' and language 'fitted to their respective importance.' Good sense arises from steady attention to subject; overly ornate or trivial language mismatched to content undermines the poem. Revise to ensure diction matches significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary connections between feelings and particular words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not habitually attach feelings to words by caprice; such arbitrary associations can produce ludicrous effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth admits he may sometimes have 'arbitrary connections of feelings and ideas with particular words' and warns poets and revisers to avoid repeating such private associations that don't translate to readers. If an expression seems faulty, correct it only when convinced—don't alter genuine feeling merely to appease a few critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: The principle of 'similitude in dissimilitude' as a source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in art derives importantly from perceiving similitude within dissimilitude (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological principle is cited as a main spring of mental activity and taste; poets should exploit contrast and unexpected likenesses to stimulate the mind and enrich imagery and metaphor. Use contrasting images that reveal unexpected connections to heighten aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist the era's craving for outrageous stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppose literature and performances that pander to a degrading thirst for shocking incident; favor durable moral relations and permanent objects of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth criticizes contemporary novels and theatricals for seeking extraordinary incident and stimulation. Poets should aim for works that 'interest mankind permanently' and cultivate the reader's capacity for refined, sustainable excitement rather than cheap sensational effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select characters with simple, natural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch characters whose elements belong 'rather to nature than to manners'—simple, enduring human types are more profitably contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'OLD MAN TRAVELLING', 'THE TWO THIEVES', and other sketches of simple characters; prefer characters built from elemental human traits rather than fashionable or highly mannered social types. Such characters allow clearer moral impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly judgment: decide by genuine personal feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers and critics should judge poems by their own genuine feelings, not by anticipated social judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth requests that readers 'decide by his own feelings genuinely' and avoid claiming a work is acceptable for themselves but unfit for certain classes. Cultivate accurate taste through sustained exposure to the best models; temper rash judgments and give works a fair hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious altering work to appease critics; preserve author's feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make revisions based solely on a few critics if the author is unconvinced; preserving the author's authentic feeling is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth warns that repeatedly setting aside one's own feelings to satisfy others can 'debilitate' a poet's mind. Revise when reason and conviction demand it, but avoid wholesale capitulation to external taste that costs the poem's integrity.
